title: The Resurrection: A Bible Study on the Evidence
subtitle: A five-session study weighing the historical case for the resurrection of Jesus, written for the skeptic.
summary:
This study is for the person who has decided the resurrection is a beautiful story and nothing more, for the Christian who has never heard anything to say to that person beyond "believe harder," and for the leader willing to host a room where both can speak freely. It takes the central claim of the Christian faith to the place it's most often dismissed, the question of whether it happened, and it doesn't treat the question as rude. It's the most important question there is. If a man was dead and then wasn't, everything changes. If he wasn't, Paul said our faith is futile, and he said it before any skeptic did (1 Corinthians 15:17).

The five sessions move in order. First, what the first Christians actually claimed and what they staked on it. Second, the short list of facts that most historians grant, believing or not. Third, the natural explanations, each put at its strongest and then tested. Fourth, the awkward detail of the women at the tomb. Fifth, what it would mean if it's true.

No study can hand anyone certainty in a box. History doesn't deal in proofs, only in probabilities weighed with care. What this one offers is a case strong enough that a thinking person can rest some weight on it without giving up their mind, and a room where nobody will be pushed to decide before they're ready.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, skeptics, and seekers

sessions.title: The Claim That Will Not Die
sessions.aim: To hear what the first Christians actually claimed, with the familiarity scraped off, and to see what they staked on it, while granting from the start that a man rising from the dead is an extraordinary claim that deserves hard scrutiny.
sessions.summary:
We've heard the word resurrection so often it has gone soft. It has become a season, a sunrise service, a banner of lilies. So this session hears it the way a stranger would. The first Christians didn't say Jesus lived on in their hearts or that his teaching outlasted him. They said a man who was publicly executed and buried was bodily alive three days later, that they ate with him and touched him.

The skeptic's first instinct is the right one. Dead men don't rise, in our experience or in theirs, and someone who won't believe it on first hearing isn't closed-minded. They're being sensible. But look at what the first Christians did with the claim. They didn't hold it loosely as an inspiration. Paul wrote that if Christ has not been raised, the faith is empty and the dead are simply dead (1 Corinthians 15:14-18). People don't talk that way about a symbol. They talk that way about an event, with a date and witnesses, and an event can be looked into. That's what this study sets out to do.

keyScripture.why: Paul rests the whole faith on one event and says that if it didn't happen, everything he preaches is empty. He treats the resurrection as something that could, in principle, be shown false, not as a symbol that no evidence could touch.

discussion.q: When you hear the claim that a dead man walked out of a tomb, what's your gut reaction? Where do you think that reaction comes from?
discussion.behind: Get the instinct into the open before any case is made. For a skeptic it's disbelief. For a long-time believer it may be a familiarity that no longer hears how strange the claim is. Both are worth naming. Let disbelief be said out loud without anyone correcting it.

discussion.q: This study starts by agreeing that it's sensible to doubt a resurrection on first hearing. Does that change how you come into the room?
discussion.behind: This sets the tone for all five weeks. A person braced for a lecture can't think. Let people say whether they expected to be argued at, and let the room see that the case can grant that dead men stay dead and still ask what happened here.

discussion.q: Read Luke 24:36-43. Why does it matter that the claim is about a body that eats and can be touched, rather than a spiritual presence or a vision?
discussion.behind: A vague claim can't be tested. A physical one can. The early Christians made the harder, riskier claim, which is odd behavior for people inventing a religion. Let the group notice that Jesus invites them to touch and see.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:12-19. Paul says that if Christ hasn't been raised, the faith is futile. Why would someone build a movement on a claim that could bring it down?
discussion.behind: Help the room see that Paul hands his critics the very lever that could topple the faith. That isn't how people talk about a myth they made up. It's how they talk about something they believe really happened and could be checked.

discussion.q: Where have you assumed, as a believer or as a skeptic, that the resurrection could only be believed or rejected, and never actually examined?
discussion.behind: Many people on both sides treat faith and evidence as separate rooms. Name that assumption and ask the group to set it aside for five weeks. Go first if the room is slow.

objections.objection: A man rising from the dead is an extraordinary claim, and extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. No amount of old testimony could clear that bar, so the question is settled before it starts. Dead men stay dead.
objections.response: It's a good principle, and nobody here should pretend otherwise. Dead men staying dead is exactly why the disciples didn't believe at first, why Thomas wanted to put his fingers in the wounds, and why the women went to the tomb with spices for a corpse. They knew as well as we do that this doesn't happen. But notice what the principle asks for. It asks that the evidence be weighed, not that the answer be ruled out before anyone looks. If no evidence could ever count, the principle isn't a standard for inquiry anymore. It's a refusal to inquire. The fair form of the demand is this: show me evidence strong enough that the resurrection explains the facts better than every natural alternative. That's a fair demand, and it's the one this study tries to meet. It doesn't ask you to lower the bar, only to hold the evidence up to it.

objections.objection: Every ancient religion has miracle stories, dying and rising gods, virgin births. The resurrection is one more myth in a crowded field, and there's no reason to treat it differently.
objections.response: The comparison sounds strong until you set the stories side by side. The dying and rising gods of the ancient world, figures like Osiris, belong to the cycle of the seasons and a sacred time long ago. None of them is a named man who died under a named governor in a datable year and was then seen by people you could go and question. The Christian claim names Pontius Pilate, who really governed Judea. It names a public execution outside a real city and a list of witnesses, many still alive when it was written down (1 Corinthians 15:6). You may still conclude they were wrong. But it isn't the same kind of claim as a myth, because myths don't invite you to check the witnesses, and this one does.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If it turned out that a man really did rise from the dead, what in your life would you most want to stay the same?
sessions.practice: This week, before weighing any evidence, sit with the claim itself. Each day read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly, and notice that Paul doesn't offer the resurrection as a comfort or a symbol. He rests everything on it. Then write two things down. First, what would have to be true about the world for a resurrection to be impossible, not just unlikely. Second, what evidence, if it existed, would actually move you. Don't try to decide anything yet. The point is to find out whether your mind is open enough to weigh it at all.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, if you are there, some of us aren't sure tonight, and we won't pretend we are. Some of us have heard this claim so often we stopped hearing it, and some of us have never believed it for a moment. Give us minds willing to weigh what we've dismissed and hearts willing to be surprised. If a man rose, we want to know it. If he didn't, we don't want to build our lives on it. Lead us toward what is true, wherever that goes. Amen.
reflection: Have I ever examined the resurrection as a historical claim, or have I only accepted it or dismissed it?
What would have to be true about the world for the resurrection to be impossible, and am I as sure of that as I thought?
The first Christians staked everything on whether it happened. Am I willing to take the question that seriously, knowing the answer could cost me something either way?
sessions.teaching:
I want to start by hearing the claim as if we'd never heard it, because most of us have heard it so often that it doesn't land anymore. The word resurrection has been worn smooth. It's a season on the church calendar, a sunrise service, lilies on a table. We have to scrape that off and hear what the first Christians were actually saying, because the familiarity has hidden how strange it is.

They weren't saying Jesus lived on in the memory of his followers. They weren't saying his teaching outlasted his death, the way Socrates's teaching outlasted his. They weren't saying they had found a deeper meaning in his execution. They were saying that a man who had been publicly put to death and sealed in a tomb was bodily alive on the third day. Luke has the risen Jesus say to frightened disciples, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:39). Then he eats a piece of fish in front of them. Whatever else that is, it isn't a vague spiritual claim.

The skeptic's first reaction is the right one, and I won't make fun of it. Dead men don't rise. That's about as reliable a fact as human experience has, and it was as true in the first century as it is tonight. A person who hears this claim and won't believe it on the first telling isn't being stubborn. They're being sensible. Carl Sagan made a phrase famous: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. I think that's correct. A claim this far outside ordinary life can't be accepted on a shrug or a feeling or because Grandma believed it. It has to clear a high bar.

Plenty of thoughtful people assume this is the kind of thing you either believe or you don't, a matter of the heart that reasons can't reach. But look at what the first Christians did with it, because it cuts against that assumption. They didn't hold the resurrection the way you hold an inspiring idea, loosely and safe from disproof. They staked everything on whether it actually happened. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth about twenty years after the crucifixion, put it this way: "And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised" (1 Corinthians 15:14-15).

He keeps going. "And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (1 Corinthians 15:17-18). Think about what he has done. He has written into the foundation of the faith a clause that could destroy it. If you can show the resurrection didn't happen, he says, then I'm a false witness, your faith is worthless, and your dead are simply dead.

People don't talk like that about a myth they invented. Someone making up a religion keeps his central claim out of reach, in the world of symbols where no evidence can touch it. Paul did the opposite. In the same chapter he gives a list of people the risen Jesus appeared to, and he adds that most of them are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6). Later, standing before a king, he says, "this has not been done in a corner" (Acts 26:26). He set the claim down in history, with a place and a governor's name and witnesses, and all but dared his readers to go and ask.

So this first session doesn't prove anything. It changes the question. In the New Testament the resurrection isn't offered as a moral or a metaphor or a private comfort. It's offered as an event, and an event can be investigated. You don't have to decide tonight whether it happened. I'm not asking you to. I'm asking you to stop assuming it can't be examined, and to bring all your doubts with you next week, when we start looking at what we actually have.

scriptureStudy.note: "And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain." Paul rests the whole faith on one event and admits that if it didn't happen, the whole thing collapses.

"And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins." The claim is built so that it could be destroyed. That is how people speak about something they think really happened.

"If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied." Paul refuses a merely symbolic resurrection. If the body didn't rise, the faith isn't a beautiful idea. It's a sad mistake.

"Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have." The risen Jesus is presented as bodily, not a ghost or a vision. That's the harder claim, and the easier one to check.
"For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner." Before a royal court, Paul appeals to public events, not private revelations.

"Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe." Thomas won't believe without evidence, and Jesus meets his demand instead of scolding him (John 20:27).

"For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty." The early church itself draws the line between myth and what it saw.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants to go further, look harder at the difference between an event and a myth, since the modern habit is to file the resurrection under myth without checking the category. Scholars of ancient religion have long noted that the so-called dying and rising gods, such as Osiris or Adonis, belong to the cycle of the seasons and the fertility of the land. They're set in a time before ordinary history, and nobody claims that a particular man died on a particular date and was seen alive afterward by people with names.

N. T. Wright's large historical study The Resurrection of the Son of God (2003) argues that the Christian belief didn't come from pagan myth and didn't grow naturally out of Jewish hope either. Most Jews of the time who believed in resurrection expected all the righteous to be raised together at the end of history, not one man in the middle of it. So the Christian claim was something new, and that newness itself needs explaining. Ask the group what would make a claim count as historical rather than mythical, and then which category the New Testament claim fits, with its named witnesses, its public setting, and its invitation to be checked.

sessions.title: The Minimal Facts
sessions.aim: To lay out the short list of facts that most historians grant, Christian or not, to feel their weight when they stand together, and to hear the strongest skeptical scholar fairly before answering him.
sessions.summary:
You don't have to believe the Bible is the inspired word of God to ask the historical question, and this session doesn't ask you to. It works from a short list of facts that most scholars, believing and unbelieving, accept on ordinary historical grounds. Gary Habermas has spent decades mapping this agreement and calls the list the minimal facts.

Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. His disciples sincerely believed they saw him alive afterward. Paul, who had violently persecuted the church, turned around because of what he was sure was an encounter with the risen Jesus. James, Jesus' brother, who didn't believe in him during his life, became a leader of the church in Jerusalem. And a creed naming the resurrection and its witnesses was already being handed on within a few years of the crucifixion (1 Corinthians 15:3-7).

Bart Ehrman, one of the best-known New Testament scholars and not a believer, grants most of these and still doesn't believe. His reasons deserve a hearing. The facts don't prove the resurrection. But they're real and stubborn, and any explanation, the skeptic's included, now has to account for all of them at once.

keyScripture.why: Paul says he is passing on something he himself received. The wording marks it as a fixed tradition, and many scholars, skeptics among them, date it to within a few years of the crucifixion, while the witnesses it names were still alive.

discussion.q: This session works only from facts that most historians grant, without asking anyone to trust the Bible first. Does that change how you weigh the question?
discussion.behind: Many people assume the case for the resurrection depends on first accepting the Bible as God's word, which would make it circular. Let the room see that these facts are granted on the same grounds historians use for any ancient event.

discussion.q: The disciples said they had seen Jesus alive, said it in the city where he was killed, and several of them died for saying it. What does that tell you, and what doesn't it tell you?
discussion.behind: Keep the point narrow. It shows they weren't knowingly lying, because people don't usually die for something they know they made up. It doesn't prove the resurrection. Help the group feel the weight without claiming more than it carries.

discussion.q: Read Galatians 1:13 and John 7:5. Paul was an enemy of the church, and James was a brother who didn't believe. Why are they harder to explain than enthusiastic followers?
discussion.behind: Followers might be expected to believe. An enemy and a doubting brother had every reason not to. Something turned them, and any explanation has to account for it.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. Why does it matter so much how early this list was being passed on?
discussion.behind: Legends usually need time, often generations, to grow. A list of witnesses circulating within a few years, while they could still be asked, leaves little room for that. Next session takes this further.

discussion.q: Bart Ehrman knows this evidence as well as anyone and doesn't believe. What do you make of that? Does it unsettle you, reassure you, or neither?
discussion.behind: Let people react honestly. A case that only beats a weak skeptic proves little. Ehrman's position shows that the facts don't force the conclusion, which keeps everyone clear about what they do and don't establish.

objections.objection: Bart Ehrman grants that the disciples had experiences they believed were the risen Jesus. He's one of the most respected New Testament scholars alive, and he doesn't believe in the resurrection. If an expert who knows all this remains a skeptic, why should I conclude otherwise?
objections.response: He's exactly the right person to reckon with. Ehrman grants that Jesus was crucified, that the disciples sincerely believed they saw him alive, and that the church grew out of that conviction. What he won't grant is a miracle, and his reason isn't careless. He argues that a historian, working as a historian, can't affirm a miracle, because history deals in probabilities and a miracle is by definition the least probable explanation. That's a serious argument, but notice what it does: it doesn't weigh the resurrection against the alternatives and find it weaker. It rules it out before the weighing starts. That's a philosophical commitment, not a historical finding. If a miracle is off the table before you look, the evidence can never put it there, but then the evidence wasn't deciding. The better question is whether, with that rule set aside, the resurrection best explains the facts Ehrman himself grants.

objections.objection: People die for false beliefs all the time. Members of every movement have died sincerely for what they believed, and they were wrong. The disciples' willingness to die proves they were sincere, which nobody doubted.
objections.response: That's right as far as it goes. Sincerity doesn't prove truth, and the disciples' deaths don't prove the resurrection. But notice the narrow thing they do show. Most people who die for a belief are dying for something someone else told them. The disciples weren't in that position. They were dying for something they said they had seen with their own eyes, a body that was alive and that they had touched and eaten with. A person can die sincerely for a falsehood they were handed. It's far harder to die for something you say you witnessed if you know you witnessed nothing. So the deaths don't settle the question. They close off one explanation, the oldest one, that the disciples knew it was false and lied. The other explanations are still open, and next week we'll look at each of them.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which of these facts is hardest to fit into the story you already believe about how Christianity began?
sessions.practice: Take one fact a day and treat it the way a historian would. Write each at the top of a page: Jesus was crucified; the disciples believed they saw him alive; Paul the persecutor changed sides; James the doubting brother became a leader; the early creed was being passed on within a few years. Under each, write the best natural explanation you can, one that doesn't involve a resurrection. Make it as strong as you can, not a weak version you can knock down. By the end of the week, notice whether the natural explanations get easier or harder when you have to make them fit all five facts together.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of truth, if these facts are stubborn, keep us from flinching, and if our explanations are thin, keep us from pretending they're thick. We don't want a faith built on bad history, and we don't want an unbelief built on a rule that decided the answer before it looked. Give us patience to hold the evidence, humility to follow it, and courage to let it cost us whichever certainty it has to. Lead us toward what really happened. Amen.
reflection: Did I assume the case for the resurrection depended on trusting the Bible first? What changes when I see that the core facts are granted on ordinary historical grounds?
What's the difference between dying for a belief someone handed me and dying for something I say I saw myself?
When a scholar rules out a miracle before weighing it, is that a historical conclusion or a prior commitment? Do I do the same thing, in either direction?
sessions.teaching:
Many skeptics assume the case for the resurrection goes like this: believe the Bible because the Bible says so, and then believe what it says about Jesus. That would be circular, and they'd be right to dismiss it. But it isn't how historians work, and it isn't how tonight works. We're going to set aside the question of whether the Bible is inspired and work only from facts that most scholars, believing and unbelieving, grant on the same grounds they'd use for any event in the ancient world. Gary Habermas has spent much of his career surveying that scholarship. He calls the result the minimal facts, the things conceded even by people with no stake in the Christian answer.

The first is that Jesus was executed by crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. Nearly everyone grants this. It's reported in several independent sources, including the Roman historian Tacitus, and it's the last thing the early church would have invented. A crucified Messiah was a contradiction to Jewish ears and a joke to Roman ones. Paul himself calls it "a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles" (1 Corinthians 1:23). Nobody makes up the most embarrassing possible fact about their founder.

The second is that the disciples sincerely believed they saw Jesus alive after his death. Notice the wording. Not that he rose, which is what we're testing, but that they believed they met him. Skeptical scholars grant this too, because the disciples said so publicly, in Jerusalem, weeks after the execution, and several of them died still saying it. Sincerity doesn't prove truth, and I don't want anyone to overstate this. But it does rule out one thing. These men weren't dying for a doctrine somebody handed them. They were dying for something they said they had seen and touched. You can die for a falsehood you were told. It's a different thing to die for something you claim to have witnessed when you know you witnessed nothing. Whatever happened, they weren't knowingly lying.

The third is Paul. He wasn't a follower waiting to believe. He tells us himself: "you have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it" (Galatians 1:13). Then he switched sides and spent the rest of his life being beaten and jailed for the faith he had tried to stamp out. In letters that almost no scholar disputes, he says the reason was that the risen Jesus appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:8). An enemy who changes sides is hard to explain away. He had every reason to stay where he was.

The fourth is James, the brother of Jesus. The Gospels say plainly that Jesus' family didn't believe in him. John writes, "For not even his brothers believed in him" (John 7:5), and Mark says his family thought he was "out of his mind" (Mark 3:21). Yet after the crucifixion James is a leader of the church in Jerusalem, and the Jewish historian Josephus records that he was stoned there around AD 62. Paul's list says simply, "Then he appeared to James" (1 Corinthians 15:7). Doubting brothers don't usually become leaders of their brother's movement for no reason.

The fifth fact does the most work. Paul writes, "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:3-5). "Delivered" and "received" were the ordinary words for handing on a fixed tradition. This is something Paul learned, not something he wrote. Many scholars, including skeptical ones, trace it to within a few years of the crucifixion, likely to Paul's visit with Peter and James in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18-19). Legends need time. This was being passed on while the people it names could still be asked.

Now the strongest skeptic, not the easiest. Bart Ehrman grants most of what I've just said. He grants the crucifixion, the disciples' conviction, and the rise of the church out of it. What he won't grant is a miracle, and his reason is principled: a historian deals in probabilities, a miracle is the least probable thing there is, so a historian can never conclude one happened. Many thoughtful people hold some version of that, and it deserves respect. But look at what it does. It doesn't find a better natural explanation. It decides beforehand that one explanation isn't allowed. That's a commitment brought to the evidence, not something the evidence produced.

So I'll say exactly what these facts do and no more. They don't prove the resurrection. They stand there, granted by friend and critic, and give every explanation the same job: account for all of them at once. The crucifixion, the disciples' conviction, the enemy who changed sides, the brother who came to believe, the creed too early for legend. We've closed the door on fraud. Next week we open every other door, and we look at each one at its strongest.

scriptureStudy.note: "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received." The words for delivering and receiving were used for passing on a fixed tradition. Paul is repeating something he learned, not composing it.
"Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep." Paul points to living witnesses who could be questioned.

"Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." Paul doesn't hide that he was once the church's enemy.

"You have heard of my former life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it." In a letter almost no one disputes, Paul confirms he was a violent opponent before he changed sides.
"And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, 'He is out of his mind.'" The Gospels record, without softening it, that Jesus' own family doubted him.
"For not even his brothers believed in him." That makes James's later leadership in the Jerusalem church something that needs explaining.
"Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed." Paul says his message is the same one the first apostles preached, one early testimony rather than a later variation.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, spend time on the date of the creed in 1 Corinthians 15, the most important single piece of this session. Paul wrote the letter in the mid-50s, but he says he's passing on something he received earlier. Galatians 1:18-19 tells us that about three years after his conversion he spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem and also saw James, the two individuals named in the creed. Many scholars, including critical ones, think that is when and where he learned it.

The usual skeptical account of miracle stories is that they grow over generations, as a figure is slowly raised in his admirers' memory until the man is buried under legend. That takes time and needs the first witnesses to be gone. A creed naming living witnesses within a few years doesn't give legend much room. But be fair to both sides. The minimal facts method has critics, who point out that agreement among scholars isn't the same as truth, and that granting the facts isn't granting the conclusion. Both points are fair. The facts are early and widely granted. The conclusion is what the rest of the study has to earn.

sessions.title: The Alternatives, Honestly Weighed
sessions.aim: To take each natural explanation of the facts in turn, put it in the form its own defenders would recognize, and test it against all the evidence, so that whatever the group concludes, it gets there by weighing and not by mockery.
sessions.summary:
If the disciples weren't lying and the facts are real, something happened, and a careful skeptic has natural explanations ready. That's what a careful mind should do. This session doesn't laugh at them. It puts each one at its strongest and asks whether it accounts for all the facts at once.

The hallucination theory, that grieving disciples saw what they longed to see, is the most serious. But hallucinations happen inside one mind, while the appearances were often to groups, and grief doesn't explain an enemy like Paul or a doubter like James. The legend theory runs into the early creed. The swoon theory asks us to believe a scourged, crucified and speared man survived and convinced his followers he had conquered death. A body stolen by the disciples brings back the liars who died for a lie; stolen by anyone else, it leaves the appearances unexplained. The wrong-tomb theory has to explain why the authorities, who had every reason to produce the body, never did.

None of these is impossible. But history asks which explanation best accounts for everything together, and that's the scale the resurrection has to be weighed on.

keyScripture.why: Paul names an appearance to a large crowd at once, which is hard to square with hallucination, since hallucinations happen inside one mind. He also notes that most of them are still alive, which leaves little room for legend to grow.

discussion.q: Why does it matter that we look at each natural explanation in its strongest form rather than its weakest?
discussion.behind: A case that only beats a weak version of the alternatives has proved nothing. If the resurrection is true, it can stand beside the best rivals. If it can't, nobody should believe it. Let the group agree to that standard.

discussion.q: The hallucination theory says grieving disciples saw what they longed to see. Where is that theory strong? Where does it struggle?
discussion.behind: Grief really does produce vivid experiences, and some in the room may have had one. Give the theory its real weight. Then let people notice that hallucinations are private, while the reported appearances were often to groups, and that Paul wasn't grieving.

discussion.q: Read John 19:31-37. The swoon theory says Jesus didn't die but revived in the tomb. What would have to be true for it to work?
discussion.behind: Walk through it slowly and without mockery. A man who had been scourged, crucified and pierced would have to survive, get out of the tomb, and convince his followers he'd conquered death rather than needed a doctor.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 28:11-15. What explanation did the authorities give for the empty tomb, and what does that explanation assume?
discussion.behind: The earliest counter-story doesn't say the tomb was full. It says the body was stolen. Let the room see that the authorities, who had every reason to produce the body, never did.

discussion.q: This study claims the resurrection is the best explanation, not that it's proven. Does that make the case more believable to you or less?
discussion.behind: History deals in probabilities, not proofs. A modest claim is often easier to trust than an overclaim. Let people answer for themselves.

objections.objection: Grief makes people see things. Bereaved spouses see and hear their dead partners, vividly, and believe it completely. The disciples loved Jesus and were devastated, and they saw what their grief produced. That explains the appearances with no miracle.
objections.response: This is the strongest natural explanation there is. Grief does produce vivid, convincing experiences, and they're well documented. So ask whether it fits all the facts. Two things strain it. First, hallucinations happen inside one person's mind, which is why two people don't share a dream. The earliest sources report appearances to groups: to the twelve together, and to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:5-6). A grieving group might each have their own experience, but they don't all see the same figure and hear the same words. Second, grief explains people who loved Jesus. It doesn't explain Paul, who wasn't mourning him but hunting his followers, or James, who hadn't believed in him. Visions in grief comfort those who loved the dead. They don't usually turn enemies into apostles.

objections.objection: Stories grow in the telling. A man dies, his followers honor him, and over the years the legend swells until an ordinary teacher becomes a risen god. That's how religious legends form.
objections.response: As a general account of how legends grow, that's right. They grow slowly, over generations, once the first witnesses are gone. The question is whether the resurrection had that kind of time, and the evidence says it didn't. The claim isn't found only in late documents written long after everyone had died. It's fixed in the creed of 1 Corinthians 15, which Paul received and passed on, and which many scholars date to within a few years of the crucifixion, while the witnesses were alive and in the city where it happened. So the legend theory doesn't fail because legends aren't real. It fails because this one would have had to form fully, within a few years, among eyewitnesses, in Jerusalem. That isn't how legends work.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Of all the natural explanations, which do you most want to be true? Is it the evidence that draws you to it, or relief at not having to deal with the other answer?
sessions.practice: Take the five alternatives, one a day: hallucination, legend, swoon, stolen body, wrong tomb. For each, write the strongest case you can, the version its smartest defender would sign. Only then write down which of last week's facts it explains well and which it struggles with. Don't go easy on either side. By the end of the week you should be able to say, in your own words, why the explanation you favor is better than the ones you set aside.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of truth, we don't want to believe something because it comforts us, and we don't want to disbelieve something because it would cost us. Both are ways of lying to ourselves. Where we've reached for the easy explanation because the hard one frightened us, forgive us. Where we've mocked instead of weighing, forgive us that too. Give us the courage to follow the evidence past what we'd prefer, and if the best explanation is the one we've been avoiding, give us the courage to say so. Amen.
reflection: Which natural explanation did I assume settled the question? Did it hold up when I made it as strong as I could and tested it against all the facts?
Where was I tempted to mock an explanation instead of weighing it, and what does that tell me about what I'm after?
Can I say plainly why the explanation I favor accounts for the facts better than the ones I'm setting aside?
sessions.teaching:
Last week we closed one door. If the disciples weren't lying, and the facts are real, then something happened. A careful skeptic doesn't throw up his hands at that point. He looks for a natural explanation, and he should. That's what a sensible mind does: look for the ordinary account before reaching for the extraordinary one. So tonight we're going to do something a lot of Christian argument skips. We'll take each natural explanation, build it as its best defenders would, and only then ask whether it fits the facts. If the resurrection is true, it can stand next to the strongest alternatives. If it can't, I don't want you to believe it.

Start with the most serious one, the hallucination theory. The disciples loved Jesus and were shattered by his death. Grief does powerful things to the mind. Many grieving people see or hear the one they've lost, vividly enough to be completely convinced. Some of you may have had that experience. So the theory says the disciples, aching to see him again, saw what their grief produced and took it for the living Jesus. That's a strong theory, but two things strain it. Hallucinations happen inside one mind, which is why two people can't share a dream, yet the earliest sources describe appearances to groups: "he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time" (1 Corinthians 15:5-6). And grief explains the people who were grieving. It doesn't explain Paul, who wasn't mourning Jesus but hunting his followers, or James, who hadn't believed in him. Grief can comfort the people who loved the dead. It doesn't usually convert his enemies.

Next is the legend theory, that the story grew in the telling until an ordinary teacher became a risen Lord. As an account of how legends form, that's simply correct. They grow over generations, once the eyewitnesses are gone and nobody is left to say it didn't happen that way. But we saw last week that the resurrection claim was fixed in a creed within a few years, while the witnesses were alive and in the city where it all happened. For the legend theory to work, the legend would have had to form completely, almost at once, among the people who could contradict it.

Then the swoon theory, which has the virtue of being entirely natural. It says Jesus didn't die on the cross. He fainted, was taken for dead, and revived in the cool of the tomb. But follow it all the way through. This is a man who had been scourged and nailed to a cross for hours. John reports that the soldiers saw he was already dead and didn't break his legs, but "one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water" (John 19:33-34). These were men whose job was to make sure. For the theory to work, that man would have to survive, get out of a sealed tomb without help, and then convince his followers not that he badly needed a doctor but that he had beaten death. A half-dead man stumbling out of a grave stirs pity. He doesn't start a movement built on the claim that death has been defeated.

Then the stolen body. If the disciples stole it, we're back at the door we closed last week: men who suffered and died for what they knew was a fraud. If someone else took it, perhaps the tomb was empty, but that explains nothing about the appearances to the disciples, to Paul, and to James. An empty tomb with no appearances isn't Christianity. Matthew tells us that the first counter-story put out in Jerusalem was exactly this: "Tell people, 'His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep'" (Matthew 28:13). Notice that it concedes the tomb was empty.

Last, the wrong tomb: in their grief the women went to the wrong grave, found it empty, and jumped to a conclusion. That one runs into a single stubborn fact. The authorities had every reason to end this movement in its first weeks. When the apostles began saying in Jerusalem, "This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses" (Acts 2:32), the simplest answer was to walk to the right tomb and produce the body. Nobody did.

I want to be careful here, because the temptation now is to claim too much. None of these explanations is impossible. Any one of them, taken alone, can be held by a determined skeptic. But history doesn't deal in proof or impossibility. It asks which account best explains all the facts together: the crucifixion, the empty tomb, the group appearances, the enemy who changed sides, the brother who came to believe, and the creed too early for legend. Each natural theory handles some of these and breaks on others. The hallucination handles the appearances and stumbles on Paul and James. The legend handles the growth of the story and stumbles on the creed. The swoon and the theft and the wrong tomb deal with the empty grave and leave the appearances untouched. The resurrection, whatever else you think of it, is the one explanation that would account for all of them at once. That isn't a proof. It's a claim about which explanation fits, and now it's yours to weigh.

scriptureStudy.note: "Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time." An appearance to a large group at once is hard to explain as hallucination, which happens inside one mind.

The chief priests pay the soldiers to say, "His disciples came by night and stole him away while we were asleep" (Matthew 28:13). The earliest counter-story doesn't deny the empty tomb. It explains it as theft.

"But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water." Professional executioners confirmed the death.
"But these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them." The disciples weren't primed to expect a resurrection. They dismissed the first report as nonsense.

"Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away." Mary's first thought is that someone moved the body. The natural explanation was the disciples' own first instinct.
"This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses." The claim was made publicly in Jerusalem within weeks, in the one city where the body could have been produced.
"And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain." Paul won't let the faith survive as inspiring fiction if the body stayed dead.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants to go further, look at how historians reason, since misunderstanding it lets both believers and skeptics claim too much. Historians don't prove events the way a mathematician proves a theorem. They compare explanations of the evidence and ask which accounts for it best, with the fewest strained assumptions and the widest reach. This is often called inference to the best explanation.

N. T. Wright argues in The Resurrection of the Son of God that the rise of the early church, with its new and specific belief, needs a sufficient cause, and that the empty tomb and the appearances together supply one, though neither would be enough alone. Bart Ehrman argues that a miracle, being the least probable event, can never be the historian's conclusion. Set the two side by side and the disagreement becomes clear. Wright is asking which explanation fits the evidence best. Ehrman is saying one candidate is disqualified before the comparison begins. That's finally a question about whether the supernatural is allowed on the table, which each person brings with them. The philosopher David Hume made the classic case against believing reports of miracles in 1748, and it's worth reading. Then ask the group: is one extraordinary event that explains all the facts simpler, or more complicated, than a separate ordinary explanation for each fact?

sessions.title: The Empty Tomb and the Women
sessions.aim: To look closely at a detail no inventor would have chosen, that women were the first witnesses to the empty tomb, and to weigh what historians call the criterion of embarrassment, while being clear that no single detail settles the question.
sessions.summary:
All four Gospels agree on an awkward detail: the first witnesses to the empty tomb were women. In the first-century world, Jewish and Roman, women's testimony was widely discounted, and in some legal settings it wasn't accepted at all. If you were inventing a story to persuade that world, you wouldn't make your first witnesses the people it wouldn't believe. You'd choose Peter and John.

Historians call this the criterion of embarrassment. A detail that is awkward for the people preserving it is more likely to be genuine, because nobody invents a problem for themselves. The women aren't the only example. The disciples run away. Peter denies Jesus three times. The first reaction to the empty tomb is fear and doubt, and the apostles dismiss the women's report as "an idle tale" (Luke 24:11).

This criterion can be stretched, and an empty tomb isn't the same as a risen man. But a story that keeps including details that hurt its own case reads more like testimony than like something made up to persuade.

keyScripture.why: The apostles dismiss the women's report as nonsense. The detail is doubly awkward for a writer trying to persuade: the witnesses are ones that culture discounted, and the leaders of the church don't believe them.

discussion.q: Read Mark 16:1-8. If you were making up a story to persuade first-century readers that a man rose from the dead, who would you choose as your first witnesses? Why didn't the Gospel writers?
discussion.behind: Let the group feel the strangeness. Someone inventing a story for credibility would pick men of standing. The Gospels do the opposite, which is hard to explain unless the women really were first and the writers felt bound to say so.

discussion.q: Where else in the Gospels do you see details that make the heroes look bad: the disciples running, Peter denying, the first reaction being fear?
discussion.behind: Help the group see the pattern. The Gospels keep details that hurt their own leaders and their own case. That's how testimony behaves when it's tied to what happened.

discussion.q: Why might it make the case more believable, not less, to admit that this one detail doesn't settle the question?
discussion.behind: A case that admits the limits of each argument is easier to trust than one that treats every point as a knockout. The women are one weight on the scale, not the whole scale.

discussion.q: Read Luke 24:1-12. What surprises you about how the apostles respond to the women?
discussion.behind: They don't believe them. Peter runs to check. Let people notice how odd that is in a book meant to strengthen faith.

discussion.q: Before this study, what did you assume the Gospels were? Has reading them closely changed that at all?
discussion.behind: Many skeptics expect the Gospels to read like propaganda. Let people say what they assumed and whether the texture of the texts fits it. No one has to change their mind tonight.

objections.objection: The criterion of embarrassment is a circular tool. Apologists call a detail embarrassing when it helps their case and ordinary when it doesn't. The women at the tomb may just reflect that women prepared bodies for burial, a practical detail, not a confession.
objections.response: That's a fair challenge, and the criterion can be abused. So apply it carefully. You're right that women prepared bodies, so their being at the tomb early in the morning is ordinary. But that's not the awkward part. The awkward part is that women are made the first and main witnesses to the central claim of the faith, in a culture that wouldn't credit them, and that the apostles are shown dismissing what they said. A writer controlling the story could easily have let the women find the tomb and then made Peter the first real witness. Instead the tradition keeps the women as the witnesses who matter and keeps the apostles doubting them. That's a detail that cut against the interest of the people who still preserved it, which is exactly when the criterion carries weight.

objections.objection: Even if the women were first, that only shows the disciples believed the tomb was empty. An empty tomb isn't a risen man. The body could have been moved, stolen or buried somewhere else.
objections.response: That's right, and nobody should claim more for the women than their testimony can bear. Applied here, the criterion supports one limited conclusion: that the empty tomb is an early, genuine part of the story and not a later addition. It doesn't prove a resurrection. An empty tomb fits several explanations, which is why we spent last week weighing them. So take the women's testimony for what it's worth. It strengthens one fact among several that any explanation has to cover. The resurrection stands or falls on whether it best explains the empty tomb, the appearances, Paul, James and the early creed together.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you picture the women running from the tomb, afraid and not believed, does it read like a story built to convince you, or like something nobody could leave out because it's what happened?
sessions.practice: This week read the resurrection accounts in all four Gospels: Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24 and John 20. Read slowly, with one question: what would an inventor have taken out? Mark each detail you find, such as fearful disciples, doubting apostles, women whose word wasn't trusted, confusion, and differences between the accounts that one made-up story would have smoothed over. At the end of the week, write down whether these read more like propaganda or more like testimony. Don't force an answer.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of truth, many of us thought we knew what the Gospels were before we'd really read them. Where we dismissed them unread, help us read them. Where we expected spin and found something stranger, help us stay with it. Thank you that the truth doesn't need to flatter itself, that it keeps the fearful and the doubting in the story because that's how it was. Make us people who can bear the truth's awkward edges rather than prefer a smooth lie. Lead us toward what really happened. Amen.
reflection: If I were inventing a story to persuade a skeptical audience, would I have chosen the witnesses the Gospels chose?
What's the difference between a story that protects its own credibility and one that keeps wounding it? Which kind is this?
Have I dismissed the Gospels as propaganda without reading them as testimony? What would it cost me to read them that way once?
sessions.teaching:
All four Gospels agree on a detail that gets more telling the better you know the world they were written in. The first people to find the tomb empty were women. Matthew puts it simply: "Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb" (Matthew 28:1). To a modern reader that may sound like nothing at all. But it has to be heard in its own century.

In the first-century world, Jewish and Roman, women's testimony was widely discounted. In some legal settings a woman's witness wasn't accepted at all. That wasn't a passing prejudice. It was built into law and custom. So put yourself in the place of someone inventing a story to convince that world that a man rose from the dead. You control every detail, and you're choosing your witnesses to be believed. You'd choose men of standing. You'd have Peter or John find the tomb. What you wouldn't do, if persuasion were the goal and invention the method, is make your first witnesses to the most important event in history the very people your audience had already decided not to trust. Yet that's what all four Gospels do.

Historians use a tool on all kinds of ancient sources, not just the Bible, called the criterion of embarrassment. The idea is simple. When a document keeps a detail that is awkward or unhelpful for the people preserving it, that detail is more likely to be genuine, because people don't invent problems for themselves. The most natural explanation is that they included it because they felt bound to, because it was what happened and too many people knew it.

Once you see it, you find it everywhere in these accounts. The disciples, the leaders of the movement, run when Jesus is arrested: "And they all left him and fled" (Mark 14:50). Peter, the rock of the church, denies three times that he knows Jesus, and when the rooster crows, "he broke down and wept" (Mark 14:72). When the women bring the news of the empty tomb, the apostles don't believe them. Luke says it plainly: "these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them" (Luke 24:11). Mark's account of the women ends with them running from the tomb, "for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The first reactions aren't triumph; they're fear, confusion and doubt.

That isn't how propaganda reads. Propaganda makes its founders brave and its witnesses credible. These accounts keep the cowardice, the denial, the doubt and the discounted witnesses, and they don't tidy any of it up. Many people assume they know what the Gospels are before they've read them closely: spin, a legend built to sell a religion. But when you read them as documents, they don't have the texture of invention. They have the texture of testimony, of people reporting what they remembered even when the memory was inconvenient.

The criterion can be abused, though, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. People sometimes call a detail embarrassing the moment it helps their case. Someone will rightly point out that women prepared bodies for burial, so their being at the tomb at dawn is ordinary. That's true. But the awkward part isn't that women came to the tomb. It's that women are made the first and main witnesses, the testimony the whole movement stands on, and that the apostles are shown dismissing them. A writer could easily have had the women find the tomb and then made Peter the first witness who counted. The tradition kept the women instead.

We need the same care in the other direction. This detail supports a limited conclusion: the empty tomb is an early, genuine part of the story, and the writers were reporting rather than building. It doesn't prove the resurrection. An empty tomb isn't a risen man. The body could in principle have been moved or stolen, which is why we spent last week weighing those possibilities. The women add real weight to one fact. They don't carry the whole case.

Still, it's worth noticing what kind of story this is. An invented story protects its own credibility. This one hands its central testimony to witnesses its culture would reject, shows its leaders as cowards and doubters, and keeps the fear and confusion in, apparently because that's how it happened. That doesn't settle anything by itself. But it's a real reason for a skeptic to stop dismissing these documents unread and to weigh them as testimony, on their own unflattering terms.

scriptureStudy.note: "But these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them." The apostles dismiss the women's report. Neither the witnesses nor the leaders come off well, which no one writing to persuade would choose.

"And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." Mark's tomb scene ends in fear and silence, not triumph.
"Now after the Sabbath, toward the dawn of the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb." All four Gospels put women first at the tomb.
"They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him." The first witness assumes the body was taken. Resurrection isn't her first thought.
"And they all left him and fled." The future leaders of the church abandon Jesus at his arrest, a detail that doesn't flatter them.
"And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.' And he broke down and wept." The church's leader is remembered for denying Jesus.

"And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve." The early creed lists only men as witnesses. The Gospel stories still keep the women first, which makes their place in those stories all the more striking.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants to go further, set the criterion of embarrassment beside the other tools historians use on ancient sources. They ask whether an event is reported by more than one independent source, whether it fits what else we know of the time, and whether it runs against the interests of those who preserved it. None of these settles anything alone, and careful scholars use them together.

Many scholars, including some who don't accept the resurrection, regard the women as first witnesses as meeting this test, given how women's testimony was treated in that world. Notice too that the creed in 1 Corinthians 15 names only men, while the Gospel stories keep the women. Some read that as a sign the Gospel writers were held by what was remembered, not free to choose the most persuasive list. Then hear the caution from the other side. Bart Ehrman, in How Jesus Became God (2014), questions whether Jesus was buried in a known tomb at all, and that challenge should be weighed rather than waved away. Ask the group what the women's testimony establishes, and what it can't.
