sessions.title: So What
sessions.aim: To move from whether it happened to what it would mean if it did, and to feel the resurrection as the firstfruits of a new creation, ending with the weight of the question rather than pressure to decide.
sessions.summary:
Suppose, for this last session, that the case holds and the best explanation of all the facts really is that a man was dead and then wasn't. Then the last question comes: so what? A careful skeptic says that even a proven resurrection would only be a strange ancient event with no claim on anyone today.

That would be true if it were an isolated wonder. But the first Christians didn't treat it that way. Paul calls the risen Jesus "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of a harvest that promises the rest. If one man has gone through death and come out in a body that can't die again, death isn't the wall we thought. It has a door. That's why Paul can write, "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26), and mean it as news.

The study ends here on purpose, without an altar call or pressure to decide. It leaves the weight of the question with each person. If it happened, the deepest human fear has been answered by an event, and the world isn't the closed room many of us assumed it was.

keyScripture.why: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits, the first part of a harvest that promises the rest, and names death as an enemy that will be destroyed. If that's true, the resurrection isn't a curiosity. It changes the shape of everything.

discussion.q: Suppose the case holds. A skeptic might still say, "So what? It's a strange thing that happened to one man long ago." Where is that reasonable, and where does it break down?
discussion.behind: Take the question seriously. An event, even a proven one, doesn't automatically make a claim on anyone. Then help the group see why the first Christians didn't treat it as a one-off.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 15:20-26. What does the word firstfruits mean in a farming world, and how does it change what the resurrection is about?
discussion.behind: The firstfruits were the first sheaf brought in, a sign that the rest of the harvest was coming. Paul is saying Jesus' resurrection is the first of many, which means it reaches forward to touch everyone's death, not only his.

discussion.q: If death really has a door, what would change in how you live? What would stay exactly the same?
discussion.behind: Don't press for a decision. The second half of the question often shows whether we hold the claim at arm's length even when we say we believe it. Let both believers and skeptics answer.

discussion.q: This study deliberately ends without an altar call. How does that sit with you?
discussion.behind: Some will feel relieved, some unsettled. Let both be said. Trusting people to weigh things in their own time is a form of respect, and it leaves the weight of the question with them.

discussion.q: After five sessions, where do you actually stand? What would still need to move you, in either direction?
discussion.behind: Let each person name where they are without anyone correcting them: belief, unbelief, or somewhere in between. Thank people for their candor; nobody needs to land tonight.

objections.objection: Even if you proved the resurrection happened, so what? It would be a bizarre ancient anomaly, a one-off two thousand years ago. Why should it make any claim on how I live now?
objections.response: That would be right if the resurrection were an isolated curiosity. A proven event doesn't by itself obligate anyone. So everything turns on whether it's isolated, and the first Christians insisted it isn't. Paul doesn't call the risen Jesus an exception. He calls him "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). At harvest, the firstfruits were the first sheaf brought in, and the point of them was that they weren't the only sheaf. They promised the rest. To call the resurrection the firstfruits is to say it's the first instance of something meant to spread, the beginning of a new creation, with the rest of the harvest to follow. If that's the claim, it isn't something that happened to one man long ago and stayed there. It's the first event in a sequence you're part of. You may refuse that claim, but you can't really say there isn't one.

objections.objection: This whole study has been building to a sales pitch. Five sessions of reasoning so that at the end you can press for a decision, a raised hand, a prayer. I've seen it before and I don't want to be closed like a deal.
objections.response: You've probably seen that, and you're right to distrust it. It won't happen here. There's no altar call at the end of this study, no manufactured urgency, and no pressure to decide tonight. That's on purpose. Endings that press for a decision tend to trade a slow reckoning for a quick yes that often doesn't survive the drive home. The case has been laid out as carefully as we could: facts granted, alternatives put at their strongest, limits admitted. Now it's yours to weigh, in your own time and with your own mind. A conclusion reached that way is the only kind worth reaching here.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If death really does have a door, what fear have you been managing your whole life that you wouldn't have to manage anymore?
sessions.practice: This week, don't try to decide anything. Each day, take the claim you've been weighing and hold it beside one ordinary moment: a meal, a worry, a goodbye, a fear. Ask, if a man really did rise and death really has a door, would this moment look any different? Don't push yourself toward belief or away from it. Just notice where the claim would touch your actual life if it's true, and where you keep it safely abstract. At the end of the week, write down where you stand now and what would still need to move you.
sessions.closingPrayer: God, if you are there, after these five weeks some of us are closer to thinking you might be, and some of us aren't. Some of us believe, and our belief is less thin than it was. Some of us don't, and we won't fake a faith we haven't reached. But we hope none of us can say anymore that the question is foolish or that the world is obviously closed. If a man rose, then the fear we carry deepest has an answer we didn't invent. Give us courage to keep weighing it, and to live as people who are no longer sure death has the last word. Lead all of us toward what is real. Amen.
reflection: If the resurrection happened, is it a curiosity with no claim on me, or the firstfruits of something I'm part of?
What would change in how I live if I believed death has a door? What would stay the same, and what does that gap say about how I hold the claim?
After five sessions, where do I actually stand, and am I willing to keep weighing it?
sessions.teaching:
We've spent four sessions on one question: did it happen? I've tried all along to give the skeptic his strongest moves, to put the alternatives at their best, and to admit where the evidence falls short of proof. Tonight I want to set that question down. It isn't settled beyond dispute, because history doesn't offer that kind of certainty. But there's a second question behind it that we've been saving, and in some ways it's harder.

Suppose the case holds. Suppose that when every fact is on the scale and every explanation has been weighed, the best account really is that a man was dead and then wasn't. The skeptic's last question is a fair one: so what? Even granting it happened, why should something strange that happened to one man in the first century make any claim on how I live now? It would be an anomaly, and anomalies don't obligate anyone. I agree with the logic. If the resurrection were a one-off wonder with nothing attached to it, it could be filed away with every other unexplained event and safely ignored.

So everything turns on whether it stands alone, and the first Christians were emphatic that it doesn't. They didn't treat the resurrection as a wonder. They treated it as a beginning. Paul writes, in the chapter we've lived in all along, "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). You have to know a harvest to feel that word. The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the crop brought in, and the whole point was that it wasn't the only sheaf. It was the first of many, the sign that the rest of the harvest was coming. To call the resurrection the firstfruits is to say it isn't an exception but a preview, the first event of a new creation breaking into the old one.

Then it isn't something that happened to one man and stopped. It's the first event in a sequence, and the sequence includes you. Paul draws the line all the way back to the beginning: "For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:21-22). Most of us live as though death is a wall, the final end that every life eventually hits. The claim of the resurrection is that the wall has a door, and one man has already walked through it.

That's why Paul can say what he says next and mean it as news, not poetry: "For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:25-26). Death isn't called the natural order or the gentle close of a good life. It's called an enemy, something that doesn't belong and won't last, already beaten in one tomb on one morning and waiting for its final defeat. By the end of the chapter Paul is taunting it: "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55).

I suspect some of you are bracing for what usually comes next. Studies like this build and reason and then, at the end, press: the altar call, the raised hand, the prayer to repeat before you can think again. I'm not going to do that, and it isn't a trick held back for later. Endings that press for a decision tend to cheapen the very weight they're trying to use. They trade a slow reckoning for a quick yes that often doesn't survive the drive home. A question this large deserves better than that.

I came to faith out of atheism, and I remember how sure I was that the world was a closed room with no door out of it. So here's where I'll leave you. If it happened, then the deepest fear a person carries, the fear of death that sits under all the others, has been answered. Not with a comforting idea or a philosophy or a vague hope that things will be all right, but with an event: a body that walked out of death and can't die again. And if that's true, the world isn't the sealed room it looks like.

You don't have to walk through that door tonight. You can disagree with everything I've said and leave exactly as you came, and nobody will have pushed you into anything. But after five weeks of weighing it, I don't think any of us can say the question is foolish or the answer is obvious. The tomb was empty or it wasn't. He rose or he didn't. Wherever you land, land there by weighing, freely, the way the first Christians invited people to. Jesus asked Martha a question beside her brother's grave, and he still asks it: "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?" (John 11:25-26).

scriptureStudy.note: "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep." The resurrection is the first sheaf of a harvest that promises the rest, which is why it reaches every death.
"For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." Paul sets the resurrection in the largest frame there is: the undoing of death's entry into the world.
"The last enemy to be destroyed is death." Death is named as an enemy, not the natural order, and its defeat has already begun.
"Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" Paul taunts the oldest human fear as a beaten enemy.
Jesus "was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead." The resurrection isn't an appendix to his teaching. It shows who he is.

"He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away." This is the harvest the firstfruits promised.
"I am the resurrection and the life." Jesus ties the answer to death to himself, not to a doctrine, and ends with a question, "Do you believe this?", which this study leaves with each person.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants to go further, spend time on what firstfruits and new creation mean. N. T. Wright argues in The Resurrection of the Son of God, and more simply in Surprised by Hope (2008), that the early Christians didn't think of Jesus' resurrection as a corpse coming back to ordinary life, the way Lazarus was raised and later died again. Nor did they mean the survival of a soul without a body, which was the Greek hope. They claimed something new: a body transformed and no longer able to die, the first piece of a renewed creation. That's why Paul reaches for the harvest image.

Set that beside the common modern assumption that the physical universe is a closed system and death is simply the end. The philosopher Charles Taylor, in A Secular Age (2007), describes how modern people came to live within what he calls the immanent frame, a picture of the world as a self-contained natural order, so that it no longer seems natural to look beyond it. The resurrection claim is a report that the frame isn't closed. Talk together about what's at stake in that difference, without pressing anyone toward a conclusion.

memoryVerse.text: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

leaderPrimer:
Two people may sit in this study asking the same question for opposite reasons. The skeptic wants to know whether it happened because he suspects it didn't. The widow wants to know because everything she has left rides on it. You're leading both, and the risk is that the evidence turns into a contest. Arguments for the faith attract a certain energy, scoring points and cornering the doubter, and the moment your room picks up on that, the skeptic will retreat into politeness and the widow will feel her grief has become a debate topic.

Keep the weighing fair and keep it kind. Every alternative explanation gets its strongest form before it's tested, and the skeptic at your table should regularly hear his position put better than he put it. If he wins an exchange, let him. A case that can't survive a good objection in a church basement won't survive his Tuesday either, and he knows it. Admit what history can't give. There's no proof here, only probabilities weighed with care, and Paul himself rested everything on the claim being checkable (1 Corinthians 15:17). Lead as someone weighing alongside the group, not as a prosecutor with the verdict in his pocket.

Don't forget the widow while you attend to the skeptic. Session five is hers. The resurrection isn't a won argument. It's a raised body, his and in time hers, so when the study reaches that point, let it land slowly. Some weeks the most persuasive voice in the room will be someone who is grieving explaining why she needs this to be true and isn't a fool for weighing it anyway. Let the arguments serve the hope, never the other way round.

faq.q: Is this study going to pressure me into a decision at the end?
faq.a: No. The last session ends with no altar call, no raised hands and no prayer to repeat. Endings that push for a decision tend to trade a slow reckoning for a quick yes that doesn't last. The study weighs the historical case as evidence and then leaves you free to reach your own conclusion, in your own time.

faq.q: Do I have to already believe the Bible is true for this study to mean anything?
faq.a: No. Session two works from a short list of facts that most historians grant on ordinary grounds, the same grounds used for any ancient event: that Jesus was crucified, that the disciples believed they saw him alive, that Paul and James changed sides, and that an early creed was being passed on within a few years. The study sets aside the question of inspiration so that someone who trusts no part of the Bible can still weigh the evidence.

faq.q: Isn't a resurrection just an extraordinary claim that no old testimony could support?
faq.a: The study agrees that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. It says in session one that doubting a resurrection on first hearing is sensible, and it points out that the disciples themselves didn't believe at first. But requiring strong evidence means weighing the evidence, not ruling out the answer before looking. The study asks whether the resurrection explains all the facts better than every natural alternative.

faq.q: Does the study take the skeptic seriously, or does it knock down weak objections?
faq.a: It takes on the strongest version of unbelief. Session two presents the reasoning of Bart Ehrman, a leading New Testament scholar who isn't a believer, before responding to it. Session three puts each natural explanation (hallucination, legend, swoon, stolen body, wrong tomb) in the form its defenders would recognize and doesn't mock any of them.

faq.q: What are the minimal facts, and why do they matter if they don't prove the resurrection?
faq.a: They're the short list of facts, gathered by Gary Habermas, that most scholars grant: the crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, the disciples' belief that they saw Jesus alive, the conversions of Paul and of James, and the early creed in 1 Corinthians 15. They don't prove the resurrection. They give every explanation the same task: account for all of them at once.

faq.q: What about natural explanations, like hallucination or the disciples stealing the body?
faq.a: Session three takes each one in turn and tests it against all the facts. Hallucination is the most serious, but it struggles with appearances to groups and with Paul and James. Legend runs into the early creed. The swoon theory asks a scourged, crucified and speared man to survive and convince his followers he had conquered death. Theft either brings back liars who died for a lie or leaves the appearances unexplained. The wrong tomb has to explain why the authorities never produced the body. None is impossible, but the study asks which explains everything together.

faq.q: Why does it matter that women were the first witnesses to the empty tomb?
faq.a: In the first-century world women's testimony was widely discounted, and someone inventing a story to persuade that world wouldn't have chosen them. Yet all four Gospels put women first, and Luke records the apostles dismissing their report (Luke 24:11). Session four claims only what this shows: that the empty tomb is an early, genuine part of the story. It doesn't by itself prove the resurrection.

faq.q: Isn't the criterion of embarrassment just a trick to prove whatever you want?
faq.a: It can be abused, and session four says so. It separates the ordinary detail (women came to the tomb because women prepared bodies) from the awkward one (women are made the main witnesses and the apostles don't believe them). The criterion carries weight only where a detail clearly worked against the people who kept it.

faq.q: Even if the resurrection happened, why should it make any claim on my life?
faq.a: Session five agrees that an isolated wonder wouldn't. But Paul calls the risen Jesus the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first of a harvest that promises the rest. If that's true, the resurrection is the beginning of something that reaches every human death, including yours. You may refuse the claim, but there is one.

faq.q: Does the study claim the resurrection is proven beyond doubt?
faq.a: No. History doesn't deal in proofs. The study argues that the resurrection is the best explanation of all the facts together, while each natural alternative is strong in one place and breaks in another. That's a claim about which explanation fits best, and the study admits the limits of each argument along the way.

faq.q: I'm a Christian who already believes. Is there anything here for me?
faq.a: Yes. A faith that has never looked at its own foundation is more fragile than it knows. You'll find words for why you believe that go beyond believing harder, and you'll be better able to sit with a doubting friend without panicking or pushing. It will also stretch you, because it asks you to take doubt more seriously than many believers are used to.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I'm not a scholar and can't answer every objection?
faq.a: You don't need to be a scholar. Every question comes with a note for the leader, and every objection comes with a response, so you're not making up arguments on the spot. Your job isn't to win debates. It's to host a fair weighing where objections are heard in full and no explanation is mocked. Saying where the evidence still feels thin to you will help more than expertise.

timeline.event: Jesus of Nazareth is crucified outside Jerusalem under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Nearly all historians, including skeptical ones, grant this.

The creed Paul later quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 (Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared to named witnesses) is being passed on. Many scholars link it to Paul's visit with Peter and James in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18-19).
Saul of Tarsus, who had persecuted the church, becomes its most tireless missionary after what he is certain was an appearance of the risen Jesus.
James, the brother of Jesus, who had not believed in him during his life, becomes a leader of the church in Jerusalem.
Paul writes 1 Corinthians, quoting the early creed, noting that most of the five hundred witnesses are still alive, and resting the whole faith on the resurrection.
James, the brother of Jesus, is stoned in Jerusalem at the order of the high priest Ananus, as recorded by the Jewish historian Josephus (Antiquities 20.200).
The four Gospels are written. They keep the awkward details: the disciples who fled, Peter's denial, the apostles' doubt, and the women as first witnesses to the empty tomb.

Josephus mentions Jesus in his Antiquities. Its line that Jesus appeared to his followers alive on the third day is widely thought to be a later Christian addition, though most scholars think Josephus did write something about Jesus there.
The Roman historian Tacitus records in his Annals that Christ was executed under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius, a hostile source confirming the crucifixion.
David Hume publishes his essay "Of Miracles," arguing that testimony can never reasonably establish a miracle. It remains the classic form of the objection Bart Ehrman makes in session two.
Gary Habermas completes his doctoral dissertation on the resurrection, where he begins the approach he later calls the minimal facts.

N. T. Wright publishes The Resurrection of the Son of God, arguing that the early Christian belief came neither from pagan myth nor from Jewish expectation, and that the empty tomb and the appearances together are needed to explain it.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for coming, especially if you came skeptical. Doubt is welcome here, and nobody will argue at you or treat you as a problem. Before we start, three things. First, you can say "I don't believe this" in this room. You can say the resurrection sounds like a myth to you, or that you have doubts you've never said out loud, and nobody's going to corner you. Second, this isn't a sales pitch. We're weighing the historical case as evidence, the way the first Christians invited people to, and history doesn't deal in proofs, only in the best explanation of the facts. Third, none of us is here as an expert. We're weighing this together. Tonight we're looking at this part of the case: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone speaks. There are no wrong reactions in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at this part of the case. Now let's bring it down to earth and ask what it would actually mean for how we think and live if this is true. That's where it stops being a debate and becomes something we have to do something with, or decide not to.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, and if it doesn't feel settled, that's all right. This study deals in the best explanation of the evidence, not in proof. Take tonight's part of the case into your week. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions without forcing a conclusion either way. If you're carrying a real doubt, or a real fear underneath it, like the fear of death that sits under all of this, please don't carry it alone. Talk to me or to someone you trust here. Nobody's being asked to decide anything tonight, and nobody will be at the end. Let me pray for us before we go. If prayer isn't something you can join yet, just sit with us. Thanks for being here.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Getting started. Read the summary together, agree that doubt is welcome and nobody will be pressured, and agree to treat the resurrection as a historical claim that can be examined.
Week 2: Session 1, The Claim That Will Not Die. Hear the claim in its strangeness and agree that it's extraordinary.
Week 3: Session 2, part one. The minimal facts: the crucifixion, the disciples' conviction, and the conversions of Paul and James.
Week 4: Session 2, part two. The early creed of 1 Corinthians 15, and Bart Ehrman's case heard in full before any response.
Week 5: Session 3, The Alternatives, Honestly Weighed. Each natural explanation at its strongest, with no mockery.
Week 6: Session 4, The Empty Tomb and the Women. The criterion of embarrassment, claiming only what it shows.
Week 7: Session 5, So What. The firstfruits and the new creation, ending without pressure, with room for the fear of death to be spoken.
Week 8: Looking back. Revisit the whole case and let each person say where they now stand and what would still need to move them.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together. The claim in its strangeness, and the facts most historians grant, including Bart Ehrman's case.
Week 2: Session 3, The Alternatives, Honestly Weighed. Each natural explanation at its strongest, tested against all the facts.
Week 3: Session 4, The Empty Tomb and the Women. The criterion of embarrassment, claiming only what it shows.
Week 4: Session 5, So What. The firstfruits and the new creation, then a short time for each person to say where they stand.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, The Claim That Will Not Die.
Week 3: Session 3, The Alternatives, Honestly Weighed.
Week 4: Session 4, The Empty Tomb and the Women.

bibliography.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Wright's large historical study (2003), arguing that the early Christian belief came neither from pagan myth nor from Jewish expectation, and that the empty tomb and the appearances together are needed to explain it. Behind sessions 1, 3 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Risen Jesus and Future Hope
bibliography.author: Gary Habermas
bibliography.note: Habermas (2003) on the minimal facts approach and what the resurrection means for Christian hope. Behind session 2.

bibliography.title: The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus
bibliography.author: Gary Habermas and Michael Licona
bibliography.note: Habermas and Licona (2004) set out the minimal facts in plain language. The most useful single book for a leader preparing session 2.

bibliography.title: How Jesus Became God: The Exaltation of a Jewish Preacher from Galilee
bibliography.author: Bart D. Ehrman
bibliography.note: Ehrman (2014) grants that the disciples believed they saw Jesus alive and explains why he doesn't accept a miracle. Read it as the strongest skeptical case, not as this study's position.

bibliography.title: The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach
bibliography.author: Michael R. Licona
bibliography.note: Licona (2010) on how historians weigh explanations, and a long test of the resurrection against its alternatives. For the leader preparing session 3.

bibliography.title: Who Moved the Stone?
bibliography.author: Frank Morison
bibliography.note: Morison (1930), a journalist who set out to write against the resurrection and changed his mind. A readable story, not a scholarly authority.

bibliography.title: Miracles
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis (1947) on whether miracles can be ruled out before looking at the evidence, the question underneath Ehrman's objection in session 2.

bibliography.title: A Secular Age
bibliography.author: Charles Taylor
bibliography.note: Taylor (2007) on how modern people came to see the world as a self-contained natural order. It helps explain why the resurrection claim sounds the way it does today. Behind session 5.

bibliography.title: Cold-Case Christianity
bibliography.author: J. Warner Wallace
bibliography.note: Wallace (2013), a former homicide detective, applies the logic of evidence and eyewitness testimony to the Gospels. A popular treatment, best read alongside the scholarship.

bibliography.title: Jesus and the Eyewitnesses: The Gospels as Eyewitness Testimony
bibliography.author: Richard Bauckham
bibliography.note: Bauckham (2006) argues that the Gospels rest on the testimony of named eyewitnesses. Useful background for session 4.

bibliography.title: Surprised by Hope: Rethinking Heaven, the Resurrection, and the Mission of the Church
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Wright (2008) on the resurrection as the beginning of new creation rather than the escape of a soul. Behind session 5.

furtherReading: The Resurrection of the Son of God, N. T. Wright, for the full historical argument.
The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus, Gary Habermas and Michael Licona, for the minimal facts set out plainly.
How Jesus Became God, Bart D. Ehrman, to hear the strongest skeptical scholar in his own words.
Surprised by Hope, N. T. Wright, for more on what the resurrection means as the beginning of new creation.

glossary.definition: The claim that Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and buried, was bodily alive again on the third day, not as a ghost or a symbol but as an event that could in principle be investigated.

Gary Habermas's name for the short list of facts most scholars grant, believing or not: the crucifixion, the disciples' belief that they saw Jesus alive, the conversions of Paul and James, and the early creed.
The summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-7 that Paul says he received and passed on: Christ's death, burial, resurrection and appearances. Many scholars date it to within a few years of the crucifixion.

The historian's rule of thumb that a detail awkward for the people preserving it is more likely to be genuine, since people don't invent problems for themselves. Used in session 4 for the women at the tomb and the disciples' fear and doubt.
How historians reason: comparing explanations of the evidence and asking which accounts for it best, rather than proving an event the way a theorem is proved.
The idea that grieving disciples saw what they longed to see. Session 3 treats it as the strongest alternative and notes that it struggles with appearances to groups and with Paul and James.
The idea that Jesus didn't die on the cross but revived in the tomb. Session 3 tests it against the condition a scourged, crucified and speared survivor would be in.
Paul's word for the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:20): the first sheaf of a harvest, which promises the rest. It marks the resurrection as the first of many, not an isolated wonder.
The Christian hope that the resurrection begins the renewal of all things: a transformed body that can't die again, not a corpse brought back to ordinary life and not a soul set free from its body.
Charles Taylor's phrase in A Secular Age for the modern picture of the world as a self-contained natural order with nothing beyond it. The resurrection claim is a report that the frame isn't closed.

The principle, made famous by Carl Sagan, that an extraordinary claim needs extraordinary evidence. The study accepts it, and insists that it means weighing the evidence, not ruling the answer out before looking.

quoteCards: Paul handed his critics the lever that could topple the faith: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile. Nobody talks that way about a myth they invented.
Dead men don't rise. Doubting a resurrection on first hearing is sensible. The question is whether the evidence clears the bar.
You can die for a falsehood someone told you. It's much harder to die for something you say you saw, if you know you saw nothing.
Legends grow over generations. This claim was fixed within a few years, among the eyewitnesses, in the city where it happened.
If you were inventing a story to persuade the ancient world, you wouldn't make your first witnesses the people it refused to believe. The Gospels did.
An invented story protects its own credibility. This one keeps the fearful disciples, the denying leader and the doubting apostles, apparently because that's how it was.
The resurrection isn't offered as a moral or a metaphor. It's offered as an event, with a place and witnesses, and an event can be investigated.
If one man has gone through death in a body that can't die again, death isn't a wall. It has a door.
